idiom_name: os.setresuid / setgroups drop, subprocess(user=, group=, extra_groups=, umask=), resource.setrlimit
implementation_notes: The standard library provides the primitives but no model: a process drops with os.setresuid/os.setresgid/os.setgroups (or the narrower os.setuid), and children start with the identity their job needs through subprocess.Popen(user=, group=, extra_groups=, umask=) - POSIX-only, added in 3.9. Two documented traps decide whether the drop is real: the documentation warns that specifying user does not drop existing supplementary group memberships, so extra_groups=() must be passed to reduce the group set for security purposes, and preexec_fn is explicitly not safe to use in the presence of threads, which is why the user, group, extra_groups and umask parameters exist. In-process narrowing (a module's __all__, a typing.Protocol that names two methods, underscore-private attributes) is convention plus static analysis rather than enforcement, and any library imported before the drop keeps the authority it had when it opened its files, sockets or connection. The classic policy-object form is justified where authority is per-request data inside one long-lived worker - and that is exactly the arrangement where one process holds every tenant's authority at once.
code_sketch:
import os, subprocess

os.setgroups([])                        # supplementary groups carry rights too
os.setresgid(-1, gid, gid)
os.setresuid(-1, uid, uid)              # saved-set is gone: not re-acquirable

subprocess.run(["/usr/local/bin/job", path], check=True,
               user="jobs", group="jobs", extra_groups=(), umask=0o027)
pitfalls: user= alone is not a drop: the documentation notes that it does not remove supplementary group memberships, so pass extra_groups=() (and a restrictive umask=) for a child that must not inherit group rights.

preexec_fn is documented as not safe to use with threads, and deferring the drop into it risks a fork-time deadlock in the child - use the user, group, extra_groups and umask parameters instead, and check the return of any direct syscall wrapper.

Imports run with the parent's authority and are cached: a module imported before the drop stays loaded, and anything already holding a file, socket or database connection keeps the access it obtained at import time, so drop before importing code that touches untrusted input or before forking.
A failed drop is easy to ignore: os.setuid raises OSError for IDs the process may not assume, and code that only logs it continues as before - CWE-250 documents exactly this shape of bug.
